analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security benefits and funds it by phasing the payroll tax onto income above the annual cap.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from May 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits in several ways: it increases the benefit formula for lower and middle earners, bases annual cost-of-living adjustments on a new inflation index that tracks what seniors actually buy, and gives widows and widowers in two-income households a larger survivor benefit. It also protects SSI recipients from losing benefits when their Social Security checks rise. To pay for it, the bill phases in the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax on earnings above the annual cap, so that by 2029 all wages and self-employment income are taxed.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security retirees and disabled beneficiaries, especially lower and middle earners, would get higher benefits and a cost-of-living adjustment keyed to senior spending. Widows and widowers in two-income households would get a survivor benefit of at least 75% of the couple's combined benefits. SSI recipients would keep their full SSI payments when their Social Security benefits rise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, widows, SSI recipients

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the first 'bend point' factor in the benefit formula from 90% to 95% (phased in from 2029 to 2033) and increases the first bend point by 1% a year up to 15% by 2044, which raises benefits most for lower- and middle-earning retirees and disabled workers.

Starting with the 2024 cost-of-living computation, annual Social Security increases would be based on a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics would publish to track prices for goods retirees typically buy, such as health care — an index that generally rises faster than the standard index.

Widows and widowers would receive the greater of the deceased spouse's benefit or 75% of the couple's combined benefits, replacing a formula that often leaves surviving spouses in two-income households with a much smaller check.
When Social Security benefits rise under the bill, SSI benefits for low-income aged and disabled people would not be reduced to offset the increase.

People who first qualify for benefits after 2029 would also have 5% of their earnings above the taxable maximum counted toward their benefit, giving high earners back a small share of the extra tax they pay.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people whose earnings exceed the annual Social Security taxable maximum (roughly $160,000 in 2023) would pay the 12.4% payroll tax on income above that cap, phased in fully by 2029. Employers would owe the matching 6.2% share on above-cap wages. High earners would get some of this back through the 5% surplus-earnings benefit credit, but far less than they pay in.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax increase lands on workers and small-business owners with income above the cap, including many self-employed professionals, and would raise labor costs for employers on above-cap pay.
High earners get only 5% of above-cap earnings counted toward their benefits, so they pay far more in new tax than they receive back.

The benefit formula improvements do not begin until 2029, while the new cost-of-living index and the first payroll tax increase start sooner, so most of the new revenue is collected before most of the new formula benefits arrive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are broad and progressive, and they are paid for directly by the payroll tax change rather than by borrowing, so the bill is internally funded. The main costs fall on the roughly 6% of workers with earnings above the cap, who receive only a small share back in benefits. The strongest good-faith objection is that a full cap lift raises taxes on upper-middle earners and small-business owners during the phase-in years before the benefit formula improvements take effect.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce Committees in May 2023, and neither committee ever scheduled a markup or vote; in December 2024, weeks before the Congress ended, it was referred to subcommittees, where it died.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee.
The Ways and Means Committee, which handles Social Security legislation, took no action on the bill for over a year and a half.

On December 17, 2024 — weeks before the 118th Congress ended — the bill was referred to the Social Security and Work and Welfare subcommittees, a step that came too late in the session to lead to action.
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without ever receiving a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with earnings above the Social Security taxable maximum are better off, because their above-cap wages remain exempt from the 12.4% payroll tax. Employers also avoid the matching tax they would have owed on above-cap pay. Retirees, widows, and SSI recipients gain nothing, and the benefit increases the bill would have delivered never happen.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners whose above-cap wages stay untaxed

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were House Democrats, while the Republican-controlled committees never scheduled action, so the bill advanced nowhere without any bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Households with earnings above the Social Security taxable maximum
industries.note: The bill would phase in the 12.4% payroll tax on all wages above the annual cap by 2029, recovering only 5% of above-cap earnings as additional benefits. The added revenue funds benefit increases for lower- and middle-income retirees.

Self-employment income above the cap would be taxed on the same phase-in schedule as wages, reaching full taxation by 2029. Self-employed people currently stop paying the 12.4% tax once they pass the cap.
Employers pay a matching 6.2% Social Security tax on covered wages, so extending coverage above the cap raises payroll costs on businesses with high-earning employees.

industries.industry: Retirees, disabled beneficiaries, and SSI recipients
industries.note: Benefit formula increases, a senior-weighted inflation index for cost-of-living adjustments, larger survivor benefits, and SSI protection all raise or protect the checks ordinary beneficiaries receive.
